Northern hawk-owl (Surnia ulula) eggs are incubated within a relatively narrow thermal window. While detailed laboratory studies of this species are scarce, data from captive breeding programs indicate that successful embryonic development proceeds when eggs are maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Under these conditions, the incubation period, or age at hatching, is approximately 27.5 days [ab = approximately 27.5 days], a duration broadly consistent with that of other medium- at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]sized strigids. Hatchlings emerge at a modest wet weight of 18 grams [Wwb = 18 grams], reflecting the altricial state typical of owl neonates. This initial body mass represents a significant investment relative to the egg content but is minimal compared to the eventual adult size. The hatchling is entirely dependent on its parents for thermoregulation and feeding. These tiny chicks, weighing just over half an ounce, exhibit rapid early growth fueled by the yolk reserves remaining at hatching and the onset of highly efficient parental provisioning. The precise control of incubation temperature is critical; deviations from 36 °C can prolong the incubation period or reduce hatching success rates significantly.

Following hatching, the nestling chick enters a phase of rapid mass gain. The initial weight of the newly hatched individual is recorded at 21.8 grams [Ww0 = 21.8 grams], and this value serves as the baseline from which all subsequent growth is measured. This mass quickly increases as the parents deliver a steady supply of small mammals, primarily voles and shrews. The downy chick develops rapidly, with feathers beginning to emerge through the natal down within the first two weeks. Under the thermal conditions that typically characterize the active metabolic period of these diurnal owls (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), a developmental milestone known as fledging occurs relatively early. The time since birth at fledging, defined as the age at which the nestling achieves its first sustained flight, is approximately 30 days [tx = approximately 30 days]. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]This developmental pace is accelerated compared to many strictly nocturnal owls, possibly reflecting the higher predation pressure faced by diurnal nestlings. At fledging, the young hawk-owl is still provisioned by its parents for several weeks, but its ability to fly marks a critical step toward independence.

Continued growth and development after fledging culminates in physiological maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, occurs at a distinct age. Under standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which is representative of the body temperature of an active hunting adult, the time since birth at puberty is 90 days [tp = 90 days]. This relatively early maturation, within three months of hatching, is characteristic of a species adapted to high-latitude, strongly seasonal environments where the breeding window is brief. However, attaining physiological reproductive capacity does not immediately lead to successful reproduction. Young hawk-owls must first establish territories and secure adequate food resources before they can breed. The initiation of the first reproductive attempt typically occurs significantly later. The time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female lays her first clutch of eggs, is documented at 365 days [tR = 365 days] under the same thermal conditions of 40.2 °C, meaning first breeding is generally deferred until the second calendar year of life.

Field studies and morphological analyses of museum specimens have established that the ultimate wet weight for females, representing the maximum adult body mass, reaches 332 grams [Wwi = 332 grams]. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males peaks at a notably lower 291.5 grams [Wwi = 291.5 grams]. This roughly 14% difference in mass is consistent with the reverse size dimorphism common among raptors, where the larger female is hypothesized to be better equipped for incubation and defense of the nest against predators and conspecific intruders. The smaller male, more agile in flight, is arguably more efficient at capturing the small rodent prey that constitutes the bulk of the species' diet during the breeding season. Maximal longevity in this species, based on long-term banding data and captive records, reaches 16 years. This corresponds to a maximum lifespan of 5,840 days [am = 5,840 days] under optimal conditions maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a substantial duration for a bird of this size class.

Reproductive investment in Northern hawk-owl is directly tied to the abundance of microtine rodent prey, leading to substantial annual variation in output. The clutch size typically ranges between 3 and 9 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = between 3 and 9 eggs per nesting attempt]. In peak vole years, larger clutches of eight or nine eggs are common, whereas in poor years pairs may forgo breeding entirely. Regardless of clutch size, the species is strictly single-brooded, producing only 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year] under the typical thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Combined, this yields a maximum reproductive rate of 3 to 9 offspring produced annually [Ri = 3 to 9 offspring produced annually]. This reproductive strategy, characterized by high fecundity in good years but a complete failure to breed in poor years, is a classic example of an irruptive, prey-specialist predator. The annual energy and time commitment to a single, large brood is considerable, requiring the male to provision both the incubating female and the rapidly growing nestlings for several consecutive months during the short Arctic and sub-Arctic summer.
